_comment: Shared cases for the watcher-liveness rule (#623), specified in
Two implementations exist on purpose: the verdict is a function of *now*, so it
decays between fetches and has to be derived where it is displayed — the third
category of ADR-0011. Neither copy is trusted; both are proved against this list,
Timestamps are RFC3339 and parsed strictly on both sides: Go's time.Parse rejects
a date without a time, and Date.parse would happily accept one, which is the kind
of silent disagreement this file exists to catch.

verdict.why: a beat two seconds ago is live
the threshold itself still counts as live
one second past it does not
a timestamp that will not parse is its own verdict, not silence
a date with no time is not RFC3339 — Go rejects it and so must the browser
a beat in the future is not stale; only elapsed time makes it so

fleet.why: one machine of three stopped: an alarm that names it
two stopped are both named, in a stable order
a machine that never beat is reporting on hooks alone, which is a choice
but a fleet with nothing beating at all is still an alarm
fleet.detail: not reporting · statuses may be frozen

fleet.why: an unreadable heartbeat names its own cause, not the machine's
mixed causes read as the broader one, and every name is listed
an empty fleet has nothing beating, which is the same alarm
